newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian politicians fear guerrilla revenge.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian politicians fear guerrilla revenge.

text.p: Threats of reprisal made by an exiled guerrilla spokesman have sown unease among Peruvian politicians, just a week after crack troops crushed Tupac Amaru rebels to end Latin America's longest hostage siege.

President Alberto Fujimori turned a massive loss of face into one of the biggest victories of his political career last week, when elite commandos stormed into the Japanese ambassador's Lima residence.
All but one of the 72 hostages held for 126 days were freed alive. All 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas were killed.
But politicians still fear the MRTA, reeling but not dead, may launch desperate attacks in an ugly mood of revenge.

"Danger is imminent. If preventative measures are not taken, the MRTA is going to grow and could take revenge by trying to assassinate political figures," said Alejandro Santamaria, of the leftist American Popular Revolutionary Alliance Party.

Congressman Genaro Colcharo of the governing Change 90 Party agreed, warning that the MRTA or its bigger guerrilla rival, the Maoist Shining Path, could try to strike a blow to dent the government's victorious new image.
"We should join forces to boost security for people in public office," Colcharo said.
The bloody war waged by leftist guerrillas against the Peruvian state since the 1980s has left at least 30,000 dead and cost the economy an estimated $25 billion.

Fujimori's big early successes against the guerrillas led many observers to hope the rebels, including the MRTA, were defeated. But the MRTA's spectacular assault to capture the Japanese ambassador's residence in December showed they could still mount a military-style operation.

Imprisoned MRTA rebels in Bolivia and the MRTA's spokesmen in Europe, the blind Isaac Velazco who speaks to the media and to the public via an Internet page, declared the movement is regrouping under a new leader, Hugo Avellanada.

"The subversives who are spreading propaganda abroad should be extradited because they are causing great damage to the country and are trying to damage the image of the Peruvian state," said Popular Action Congressman Javier Alva.

Hundreds of MRTA guerrillas are in Peruvian prisons and the guerrilla's former leader, Nestor Cerpa, was gunned down last week. But this time Fujimori is steering clear of claiming absolute and final victory over the rebels, as he did after the 1992 capture of Shining Path leader Abimael Guzman.
Experts estimate the MRTA has only 200 guerrillas left, hiding in Peru's eastern jungle. But they fear that may be enough to cause damage.
Before grabbing the Japanese ambassador's residence, the MRTA planned an even more spectacular operation in 1995, when security forces foiled a plot by the group to sieze Congress.

A young American woman, Lori Berenson, was among those accused of planning to take Congress and was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1996 for treason and for being an MRTA leader. She admitted sympathising with the MRTA, but rejected charges of participating in guerrilla activity.
Many fear the guerrillas will never be totally defeated until the impoverished half of the population of Peru sees its lot improve.

"Bringing peace is not about worrying about chasing after terrorists, but effective action to put into place the means and resources needed to solve the social and economic crisis in Peru," Congressman Aldo Estrada of the Union for Peru said.
